recipe.history:
Chives — Allium schoenoprasum — are the most delicate members of the allium family, a genus that also includes onions, garlic, leeks, and shallots, and they occupy a special place in the culinary traditions of Europe and China, where they have been cultivated for thousands of years. In Chinese cooking, both common chives and garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) appear in dumplings, stir-fries, and egg dishes, prized for their fragrant, grassy intensity. In European cuisine, chives are among the canonical fines herbes of classical French cooking — alongside tarragon, chervil, and flat-leaf parsley — used to finish dishes with a bright, onion-forward freshness that heat would destroy. The ancient Greeks and Romans were familiar with chives as a medicinal and culinary herb, and they appear in medieval European herbals as a plant with both culinary and apotropaic properties. The pea, meanwhile — Pisum sativum — is one of humanity's oldest cultivated vegetables, grown in the Near East for at least ten thousand years, treasured in medieval Europe as a winter staple when dried, and celebrated in spring as a luxury vegetable when fresh. Together, chive and pea represent the green, vegetal freshness of spring itself.

Chive oil — made by blanching chives briefly and blending them with neutral oil — emerged as a fine dining technique in the 1990s and early 2000s, primarily in the orbit of modernist and nouvelle cuisine kitchens, as a way to capture the bright chlorophyll of fresh herbs in a stable, drizzleable form. Its migration from tasting-menu courses to the burger world reflects the broader democratization of fine-dining techniques that has characterized American food culture in the twenty-first century. Pea shoots — the tender young tendrils and leaves of the pea plant — found their way into salads and sandwiches as the farm-to-table movement popularized ingredient sourcing from local farms, where pea shoots are an early-season crop. On a burger, pea shoots provide a textural freshness — slightly grassy, slightly sweet — that lettuces cannot quite match, and chive oil ties the whole construction together with a vivid green thread.

I planted chives in a pot on my apartment windowsill years ago, mostly because they seemed like the easiest possible herb to keep alive, and I was right — they are virtually unkillable, returning every spring like an old friend. I started snipping them over scrambled eggs, over baked potatoes, over pasta with butter, and eventually I started making chive oil on Sunday afternoons as a way to preserve the excess before it went to seed. The first time I put chive oil on a burger — just a drizzle over a patty with some blanched peas on top — I thought it might be pretentious. It was not. It was one of the cleanest, most genuinely delicious burgers I had made in years, the green freshness cutting through the beef in a way that completely changed the register of the dish. The pea shoot salad came later, and it made everything better.

Philosophically, the argument for medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is most compelling when the toppings are delicate. The Chive Easy Peas-Es Burger is a burger about freshness and green vitality, and it would be an act of internal contradiction to serve those vibrant toppings over a grey, overcooked patty. The pea shoots wilt at the edges of a warm patty; the chive oil pools in the meat's crevices. A medium-rare patty, yielding and warm and still rosy at its core, is the correct canvas for these toppings: it is alive in the same way the chives and peas are alive, and the harmony between them is only possible when the beef is cooked with the same respect for temperature and timing that one would apply to any other living ingredient.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
1 cup fresh or thawed frozen peas
fine sea salt and white pepper
For the herbed goat cheese spread:
fine sea salt and white pepper
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low to combine, then add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Increase to medium-high and knead until smooth and elastic, 8 minutes. Rise in an oiled bowl until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours.

2. Divide dough into 6 portions (about 140g each), shape into tight rounds, and place on parchment-lined baking sheets. Proof 40 minutes until puffy. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with sesame seeds, and bake 18 to 20 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.

3. Make the chive oil: Bring a small pot of salted water to a boil. Blanch chives for 20 seconds, then immediately transfer to an ice bath. Drain and squeeze out as much water as possible. Combine blanched chives, neutral oil, and salt in a high-speed blender. Blend on high for 2 minutes until completely smooth and vivid green. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer into a small bowl. Discard solids. The oil keeps refrigerated for up to 5 days.
4. Make the herbed goat cheese: Combine softened goat cheese, minced chives, lemon zest, and heavy cream in a bowl. Season with salt and white pepper. Mix until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the pea shoot salad: If using fresh peas, blanch in boiling salted water for 90 seconds; drain and shock in ice water. In a bowl, whisk lemon juice, 1 tbsp chive oil, and honey. Season with salt and white pepper. Toss pea shoots and peas in the dressing just before serving.

6. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes. The internal temperature must reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare, the only correct temperature for any burger. Rest on a rack for 3 minutes.
8. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

9. Assemble: Spread herbed goat cheese generously on the bottom bun. Place the medium-rare patty on top. Drizzle 1 to 2 teaspoons of chive oil directly over the patty. Pile a generous handful of dressed pea shoot salad on top of the patty. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Spread a thin layer of chive oil on the top bun. Cap and serve immediately.
